doc.title: Dave Liebman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Standing beside Shorter: stillness, embouchure and ear
summary: Next to Shorter he marvelled at his perfectly still classical embouchure and quick ear.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Very still. Everything’s correct. All this shit is happening inside. This is unbelievable. I’m standing right next to the guy. He’s tonguing. He’s doing all that shit, and there’s nothing moving, and the lip is perfectly in place. It was deep. Also, he had a great ear. As soon as you played something, he knew it. I could tell he could hear it. He might have perfect pitch. I don’t know. It sounds like to me he could play back anything, one of those guys. I’m not like that. I can’t just play it right back to you, but he sounds like he could play it right back to you. That was great. Also, he was great. There’s great stories. We’re in the hotel lobby. We landed. Wayne’s group was there, and Gomez was – Gomez had his group, I think. Richie was there for me, with me, and I’m missing – I think Jack had his own group. I forget. This was a big festival. Coltrane, live under the sky, 30 years since Coltrane died, blah blah blah. We’re the big – the Coltrane thing. And the World Saxophone Quartet, weird thing.
